step_by_step_reasoning: 1) Inventory from the whiteboard: USER, Route 53, ALB, EKS + SPOT (one dashed box), SNS, SQS. The hand-drawn oval and the M.S.1/2/3 labels are Kubernetes jobs/microservices running inside EKS, not separate services, so they are folded into the EKS node. 2) SPOT is the capacity modifier of the cluster (100% Spot nodes), so it is fused with EKS as in the world model. 3) The user is kept as the system entry point. The audio describes an internal developer platform (Orion portal) used to request environments, so the actor is typed as UserCompanyDeveloper rather than the world model's UserConsumerWeb. 4) Flow 0 (environment request): User -> Route 53 (DNS resolution of the Orion portal URL) -> ALB -> application pod on EKS. 5) Flow 1 (job state and recovery on Spot): each Kubernetes job launching a microservice sends an event to SNS, SNS fans the message out to SQS, and a replacement job watches SQS to find and finish unfinished work. The drawn arrow from the microservice area to SQS is recorded as EKS -> SQS with type meta (polling/watching). 6) The AWS Node Termination Handler is mentioned only as a component inside the cluster and is not drawn, so it is recorded in the EKS notes rather than as a node.

graph.name: OLX Autos: Internal Developer Platform (Orion) on Amazon EKS with 100% Spot Instances
graph.categories: Containers, Developer Platform, Cost Optimization, Messaging
graph.notes: OLX Autos built an internal developer platform (Orion portal) to create replica environments on demand, reducing time to market and increasing deployment velocity. Requests go through Route 53 and ALB to an application pod on Amazon EKS running on 100% Spot instances. The application creates one Kubernetes job per microservice; job state is persisted through SNS to SQS so that replacement jobs can resume unfinished work after Spot terminations. The cluster scaled from 100 to 10,000+ pods; the company operates in 11 countries.

nodes.name: USER
nodes.notes: End user of the internal developer platform. Opens the Orion portal (https://...orion) and requests a new environment, giving the environment name, business use case and business vertical.

nodes.name: ROUTE 53
nodes.notes: DNS resolution for the Orion portal; resolves to the Application Load Balancer.

nodes.name: ALB
nodes.notes: Application Load Balancer that sends the request to the Kubernetes pods.

nodes.name: EKS (SPOT)
nodes.notes: Amazon EKS as container orchestrator; all workloads run on 100% Spot instances for cost efficiency. The main application pod creates one Kubernetes job per microservice (M.S.1, M.S.2, M.S.3; a business vertical may need 70+ microservices). AWS Node Termination Handler listens for Spot termination events and drains nodes so workloads shift to another node without disruption. EKS replaces interrupted jobs. Scaled from 100 pods to 10,000+ pods.

nodes.name: SNS
nodes.notes: Receives an event whenever a job is triggered to create a microservice and fans the message out to SQS.

nodes.name: SQS
nodes.notes: Holds job state/pending work. Replacement jobs watch the queue to detect unfinished jobs (e.g. launching microservice 1) and complete them, keeping provisioning and maintenance of environments in a consistent state.

edges.notes: User opens the Orion portal URL (https://...); DNS resolution goes to Route 53.
Route 53 resolves the DNS to the Application Load Balancer.
ALB sends the environment creation request to the application pod on EKS (Spot instances), which creates Kubernetes jobs for each microservice.
When a job is triggered to create a microservice, it sends an event to SNS.
SNS fans out the message to SQS, storing the job state.
The replacement job (after a Spot interruption) watches SQS for unfinished jobs and completes the pending microservice launch.
